title: Alternating Current (AC) & EM Waves
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Mean & RMS Values, Phasor Analysis of R/L/C, Series LCR Impedance Triangle, Resonance & Quality Factor, AC Power & Power Factor, Choke Coil, Transformers, Displacement Current & Electromagnetic Waves
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: Why Does the World Run on AC Instead of DC?

Every wall socket in your home supplies a sinusoidal Alternating Voltage ($V_{\text{rms}} = 220\text{ V}, f = 50\text{ Hz}$ in India) that reverses its polarity $100$ times every second! Why go through all that trouble instead of using steady Direct Current (DC)?

Because by Faraday's Law of Induction, Transformers work ONLY on Alternating Current! Power plants step up AC voltage to $400,000\text{ V}$ so current $I = P/V$ becomes tiny, slashing transmission line heat loss ($P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R_{\text{line}}$) by factors of thousands, and then step it safely back down to $220\text{ V}$ outside your home.

How Do We Measure AC If Its Full-Cycle Average Is Zero?
• DC Ammeter / Voltmeter (Moving-Coil Galvanometer): Deflection $\theta \propto I$. Since average AC over a full cycle is zero, a DC meter connected to $50\text{ Hz}$ AC simply vibrates at **zero reading**!
• AC Ammeter / Voltmeter (Hot-Wire Instrument): Works on Joule heating ($H \propto I^2$), which is always positive whether current flows forward or backward, measuring the Root-Mean-Square ($I_{\text{rms}}$) value!

topics.title: Average (Mean) & RMS Values of AC, Pure R, Pure L and Pure C Circuits & Reactance vs. Frequency
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Average (Mean) Value & Root-Mean-Square (RMS / Virtual) Value of AC

For a sinusoidal alternating current $I(t) = I_0\sin(\omega t)$ (where $I_0$ is peak amplitude):

$$\text{1. Full-Cycle Average:} \quad \langle I \rangle_{\text{full}} = 0 \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{2. Half-Cycle Average:} \quad \boxed{I_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2 I_0}{\pi} \approx 0.637\,I_0}$$
$$\text{3. RMS (Effective) Value:} \qquad \boxed{I_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\langle I^2 \rangle} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707\,I_0, \qquad V_{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}}$$

Crucial JEE Shortcut for Composite Waveforms ($I = I_{\text{DC}} + I_1\sin(\omega t) + I_2\cos(\omega t)$):
Because cross-product averages like $\langle \sin(\omega t) \rangle = 0$ and $\langle \sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega t) \rangle = 0$ vanish over a full cycle, the RMS value of a sum of orthogonal signals is:

$$\boxed{I_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{I_{\text{DC}}^2 + \frac{I_1^2}{2} + \frac{I_2^2}{2}}}$$

topics.derivationHtml:
Calculus Proof of I_avg = 2I₀/π and I_rms = I₀/√2

1. Half-Cycle Average ($0$ to $T/2 = \pi/\omega$):

$$I_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\int_0^{\pi/\omega} I_0\sin(\omega t)\,dt}{\pi/\omega} = \frac{\omega I_0}{\pi}\left[-\frac{\cos(\omega t)}{\omega}\right]_0^{\pi/\omega} = \frac{I_0}{\pi}(1 - (-1)) = \boxed{\frac{2I_0}{\pi}}$$

2. Full-Cycle RMS Value: Since the average value of $\sin^2(\omega t) = \frac{1 - \cos(2\omega t)}{2}$ over a full cycle is $\frac{1}{2}$:

$$\langle I^2 \rangle = I_0^2 \langle \sin^2(\omega t) \rangle = \frac{I_0^2}{2} \implies \boxed{I_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\langle I^2 \rangle} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}}$$

Thus a $220\text{ V}$ AC line swings between $+220\sqrt{2} = +311\text{ V}$ and $-311\text{ V}$, which is why a $220\text{ V}$ AC shock is more dangerous than a $220\text{ V}$ DC shock, and any capacitor connected across $220\text{ V}$ AC must have a breakdown rating greater than $311\text{ V}$!

topics.title: Series LCR Circuit, Impedance Triangle, Electrical Resonance, Quality Factor (Q), Power Factor & Wattless Current
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Series LCR Circuit & The Impedance Triangle ($Z$)
Why AC Voltages Across $R, L,$ and $C$ Do NOT Add Algebraically ($V \neq V_R + V_L + V_C$):
In a series LCR circuit, the same current $I(t)$ flows through all three elements, so $V_R$ is along $I$ ($0^\circ$), $V_L$ points straight up ($+90^\circ$), and $V_C$ points straight down ($-90^\circ$). Therefore, $V_L$ and $V_C$ are $180^\circ$ out of phase and subtract directly, while $V_R$ is perpendicular to $(V_L - V_C)$!
$$\text{1. Net Supply Voltage:} \qquad \boxed{V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}} \qquad (\text{Holds for both Peak } V_0 \text{ and } V_{\text{rms}}!)$$
$$\text{2. Impedance } (Z = V/I): \qquad \boxed{Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2} = \sqrt{R^2 + \left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^2}}$$
$$\text{3. Phase Angle } \phi \text{ (by which } V \text{ leads } I\text{):} \qquad \boxed{\tan\phi = \frac{V_L - V_C}{V_R} = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}, \qquad \cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z}}$$
  • If $X_L > X_C$ ($f > f_0$): Circuit is Inductive ($\phi > 0$, voltage leads current).
  • If $X_C > X_L$ ($f < f_0$): Circuit is Capacitive ($\phi < 0$, current leads voltage).
2.2 Series LCR Resonance ($X_L = X_C$), Bandwidth & Quality Factor ($Q$)

At a specific angular frequency $\omega_0$, inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance ($X_L = X_C$), canceling each other completely:

$$\textbf{Resonant Frequency:} \quad \omega_0 L = \frac{1}{\omega_0 C} \implies \boxed{\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}}$$

At Resonance ($\omega = \omega_0$):
1. Impedance is minimum: $\boxed{Z_{\min} = R}$.
2. Current is maximum: $\boxed{I_{\max} = \frac{V}{R}}$.
3. Phase difference is zero ($\phi = 0^\circ$) and Power Factor is maximum ($\cos\phi = 1$).
4. $V_L = V_C = I_{\max} X_L = Q \cdot V$ (can be much larger than the supply voltage $V$!), while $V_R = V$.

$$\textbf{Half-Power Bandwidth } (\Delta\omega = \omega_2 - \omega_1): \quad \boxed{\Delta\omega = \frac{R}{L}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \textbf{Quality Factor (Sharpness } Q\textbf{):} \quad \boxed{Q = \frac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega} = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{\omega_0 C R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}}$$
2.3 Average Power in AC Circuits, Power Factor ($\cos\phi$), Wattless Current & Choke Coil
$$\boxed{P_{\text{avg}} = V_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}} \cos\phi = \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \cos\phi = I_{\text{rms}}^2 R = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}^2 R}{Z^2}}$$
  • Power Factor ($\cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z}$): Ratio of True Power ($P_{\text{avg}}$) to Apparent Power ($V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}$).
  • Wattless Current: The component of current $I_{\text{rms}}\sin\phi$ perpendicular ($90^\circ$) to voltage $V$, which consumes zero average power!
  • Choke Coil (Used in Fluorescent Tube Lights): An inductor of high $L$ and nearly zero resistance ($r \approx 0$), so $\phi \approx 90^\circ \implies \cos\phi \approx 0$. It limits AC current without wasting electrical energy as heat!
topics.derivationHtml:
Full-Cycle Integration Proof of Average AC Power P_avg = V_rms I_rms cos φ

Let $V(t) = V_0\sin(\omega t)$ and $I(t) = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$. Instantaneous power is $P(t) = V(t)I(t)$:

$$P(t) = V_0 I_0 \sin(\omega t)\sin(\omega t - \phi) = V_0 I_0 \sin(\omega t)\left[\sin(\omega t)\cos\phi - \cos(\omega t)\sin\phi\right]$$$$P(t) = V_0 I_0 \cos\phi \sin^2(\omega t) - \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \sin\phi \sin(2\omega t)$$

Over one complete cycle, $\langle \sin^2(\omega t) \rangle = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\langle \sin(2\omega t) \rangle = 0$, leaving:

$$\boxed{P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}V_0 I_0 \cos\phi = \left(\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\cos\phi = V_{\text{rms}} I_{\text{rms}} \cos\phi}$$

It is $V = \sqrt{60^2 + (100 - 20)^2} = \sqrt{60^2 + 80^2} = \mathbf{100\text{ V}}$!

topics.title: Transformers, Maxwell's Displacement Current & Electromagnetic Waves (Speed, E/B Ratio, Poynting Vector & Radiation Pressure)
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Transformers (Mutual Induction Between Primary $N_p$ and Secondary $N_s$ Coils)

In an ideal transformer with laminated soft-iron core, the same magnetic flux $\Phi_B(t)$ links every single turn of both coils:

$$\boxed{\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{\mathcal{E}_s}{\mathcal{E}_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p} = k_{\text{turns}}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{For Ideal Transformer } (\eta = 100\%, \; V_p I_p = V_s I_s): \quad \boxed{\frac{I_p}{I_s} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}}$$
$$\text{Real Transformer Efficiency:} \qquad \boxed{\eta = \frac{\text{Output Power}}{\text{Input Power}} \times 100\% = \frac{V_s I_s}{V_p I_p} \times 100\%}$$
  • Step-Up Transformer ($N_s > N_p$): Increases voltage ($V_s > V_p$) and decreases current ($I_s < I_p$).
  • Step-Down Transformer ($N_s < N_p$): Decreases voltage ($V_s < V_p$) and increases current ($I_s > I_p$).
  • 4 Causes of Energy Loss in Real Transformers: (1) Flux Leakage (reduced by winding coils over each other), (2) Copper / Joule Loss $I^2 R$ (reduced by using thick copper wires), (3) Eddy Current Loss (reduced by using laminated iron sheets), and (4) Hysteresis Loss (reduced by using soft iron core with narrow $B$-$H$ loop).
3.2 Maxwell's Displacement Current ($I_d$) & Properties of Electromagnetic Waves
Maxwell's Missing Piece in Ampere's Law (Displacement Current $I_d$):
While charging a capacitor, conduction current $I_c$ flows in the wires, but no charge crosses the insulating gap between the plates. However, the electric flux $\Phi_E = EA$ between the plates changes at rate $\frac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = \frac{I_c}{\varepsilon_0}$, creating a magnetic field between the plates identical to a real current!
$$\textbf{Displacement Current:} \quad \boxed{I_d = \varepsilon_0 \frac{d\Phi_E}{dt} = C\frac{dV}{dt} = I_{\text{conduction}}} \qquad \implies \qquad \boxed{\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0(I_c + I_d)}$$

The 6 Golden Equations of Electromagnetic Waves (MEMORIZE FOR JEE MAIN!):

  1. Transverse & Orthogonal Direction Rule: $\vec{E} \perp \vec{B} \perp \vec{c}$, and the direction of wave propagation is ALWAYS given by the cross product $\boxed{\hat{c} = \hat{E} \times \hat{B}}$! (Furthermore, $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ oscillate in the exact same phase, reaching maxima and zeros simultaneously!).
  2. Speed in Vacuum & Medium:
    $$\boxed{c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}} = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{In Medium } (\mu_r, \varepsilon_r): \quad \boxed{v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu_r \varepsilon_r}} = \frac{c}{n}}$$
  3. Electric-to-Magnetic Field Amplitude Ratio:
    $$\boxed{\frac{E_0}{B_0} = \frac{E_{\text{rms}}}{B_{\text{rms}}} = \frac{E(x,t)}{B(x,t)} = c \quad (\text{or } v \text{ in medium})}$$
  4. Equal Energy Partition ($u_E = u_B$): Electric field energy density $u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$ is ALWAYS equal to magnetic field energy density $u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$:
    $$\boxed{u_{\text{avg}} = u_{E,\text{avg}} + u_{B,\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2 = \varepsilon_0 E_{\text{rms}}^2 = \frac{B_0^2}{2\mu_0} = \frac{B_{\text{rms}}^2}{\mu_0}}$$
  5. Poynting Vector ($\vec{S}$) & Wave Intensity ($I$):
    $$\vec{S} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}(\vec{E} \times \vec{B}) \qquad \implies \qquad \boxed{I = \langle S \rangle = u_{\text{avg}}\,c = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 c E_0^2 = \frac{E_0 B_0}{2\mu_0}}$$
  6. Momentum ($p = U/c$) & Radiation Pressure ($P_{\text{rad}}$):
    • Completely Absorbing Surface (Blackbody, $r = 0$): $\boxed{P_{\text{rad}} = \frac{I}{c}}$, Force $F = \frac{I A}{c} = \frac{\text{Power}}{c}$.
    • Completely Reflecting Surface (Mirror, $r = 1$): $\boxed{P_{\text{rad}} = \frac{2I}{c}}$, Force $F = \frac{2\,\text{Power}}{c}$.

Order of EM Spectrum by Increasing Frequency ($f \uparrow$) & Decreasing Wavelength ($\lambda \downarrow$):
Radio Waves $\to$ Microwaves $\to$ Infrared (IR) $\to$ Visible Light (ROYGBIV) $\to$ Ultraviolet (UV) $\to$ X-Rays $\to$ Gamma ($\gamma$) Rays!
topics.derivationHtml:
Proof that Electric Energy Density Equals Magnetic Energy Density (u_E = u_B) in an EM Wave

Using $E = cB$ and $c^2 = \frac{1}{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$, substitute $E = \frac{B}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$ into the electric energy density formula $u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2$:

$$u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 (cB)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 \left(\frac{1}{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\right)B^2 = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0} = u_B$$

Thus $\boxed{u_E = u_B}$ at every point and every instant in a traveling electromagnetic wave!

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Are $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ in an EM Wave $90^\circ$ Out of Phase? NO!): Students confuse spatial perpendicularity ($\vec{E} \perp \vec{B}$ in space, $90^\circ$ geometric angle) with temporal phase! In time and space, $\vec{E} = E_0\sin(\omega t - kx)\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = B_0\sin(\omega t - kx)\hat{k}$ oscillate with ZERO phase difference ($\Delta\phi = 0$)—both reach their peaks and zero-crossings at the exact same instant!
  • Trap 2 (Vector Form of $\vec{B}$ from $\vec{E}$): Since $\hat{E} \times \hat{B} = \hat{c}$ and $(\hat{c} \times \hat{E}) = \hat{B}$, you can find the magnetic field vector $\vec{B}$ directly from $\vec{E}$ and unit propagation vector $\hat{c}$ using $\boxed{\vec{B} = \frac{1}{c}(\hat{c} \times \vec{E})}$!

conclusion: Congratulations! By completing Chapter 21: Alternating Current & Electromagnetic Waves, you have mastered the entire Electrodynamics Unit (Chapters 15 to 21)! Next, in Chapter 22, we enter Geometric (Ray) Optics.
summary:
• AC Values: $I_{\text{avg, half}} = \frac{2I_0}{\pi}$, $I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}}$; $X_L = \omega L$, $X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}$.
  • Series LCR: $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$, $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L - X_C}{R}$, $\cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z}$, $P_{\text{avg}} = V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi = I_{\text{rms}}^2 R$.
  • Resonance: $\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$, $Z_{\min} = R$, $\Delta\omega = \frac{R}{L}$, $Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}$.
  • Transformers: $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$ and $\eta = \frac{V_s I_s}{V_p I_p}$.
  • EM Waves: $c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} = \frac{E_0}{B_0}$, $\hat{c} = \hat{E}\times\hat{B}$, $u_E = u_B$, $I = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 c E_0^2$, $P_{\text{rad}} = \frac{I}{c}$ (absorbing) or $\frac{2I}{c}$ (reflecting).

LCR Impedance & Voltage$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, \quad V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$At resonance $X_L = X_C \implies Z = R$.
Quality Factor ($Q$)$Q = \dfrac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega} = \dfrac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R}\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}}$Bandwidth $\Delta\omega = \dfrac{R}{L}\text{ rad/s}$.
Average AC Power$P_{\text{avg}} = V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi = I_{\text{rms}}^2 R$Power factor $\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z}$.
EM Wave Relations$c = \dfrac{E_0}{B_0} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}, \qquad \vec{B} = \dfrac{1}{c}(\hat{c}\times\vec{E})$$\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ oscillate in phase ($\Delta\phi = 0$).
EM Intensity & Pressure$I = \dfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 c E_0^2 = \dfrac{B_0^2 c}{2\mu_0}, \qquad P_{\text{rad}} = (1 + r)\dfrac{I}{c}$$r=0$ absorbing; $r=1$ perfectly reflecting.

questions.prompt: An electric current has both a DC component and an AC component given by $I(t) = 3 + 4\sqrt{2}\sin(100\pi t)\text{ A}$. What will a hot-wire AC ammeter read when connected in series with this circuit?
questions.explanation: A hot-wire ammeter reads the RMS current: $I_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{I_{\text{DC}}^2 + \frac{I_0^2}{2}} = \sqrt{3^2 + \frac{(4\sqrt{2})^2}{2}} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\text{ A}$.

questions.prompt: In a series LCR circuit, the AC voltmeter readings across the resistor $R$, inductor $L$, and capacitor $C$ are $V_R = 80\text{ V}$, $V_L = 120\text{ V}$, and $V_C = 60\text{ V}$ respectively. What is the RMS voltage of the AC supply?

A series LCR circuit with $R = 10\,\Omega$, $L = 2\text{ H}$, and $C = 32\,\mu\text{F}$ is connected to a variable-frequency AC source. What are (i) the resonant angular frequency $\omega_0$ and (ii) the Quality Factor $Q$ of the circuit at resonance?

In an alternating current circuit, the instantaneous voltage and current are given by $V = 200\sin(100t)\text{ V}$ and $I = 2\sin\left(100t - \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\text{ A}$. What is the average power consumed in the circuit over one complete cycle?

A plane electromagnetic wave travels in free space along the $+x$-direction. At a particular point in space and time, its electric field vector is $\vec{E} = 6.0\,\hat{j}\text{ V/m}$. What is the magnetic field vector $\vec{B}$ at that point? ($c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$)

An inductor coil draws a current of $I_{\text{DC}} = 4\text{ A}$ when connected to a $20\text{ V}$ DC battery. When the same coil is connected to a $20\text{ V}$ (RMS), $50\text{ Hz}$ AC source, it draws an RMS current of $I_{\text{AC}} = 2.4\text{ A}$. What is the inductance $L$ of the coil?
questions.explanation: With DC ($X_L = 0$), resistance of the coil is $R = \frac{20\text{ V}}{4\text{ A}} = 5\,\Omega$. With AC, impedance is $Z = \frac{20\text{ V}}{2.4\text{ A}} = \frac{25}{3}\,\Omega$. Therefore, $X_L = \sqrt{Z^2 - R^2} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{25}{3}\right)^2 - 5^2} = \frac{20}{3}\,\Omega$. Since $X_L = 2\pi f L = 100\pi L = \frac{20}{3}$, we get $L = \frac{20}{300\pi} = \frac{1}{15\pi}\text{ H}$.
